source.title: Establishing Deep InfoMax as an effective self-supervised learning methodology in materials informatics
source.authors: Michael Moran; M. Gaultois; Vladimir V. Gusev; D. Antypov; M. Rosseinsky

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent and interprets a comparison of trained models as a possible example, but it does not test any of the claim versions’ predicted curves or thresholds.
record.gate_note: The authors compare supervised Site-Net models with small models trained on frozen representations and call the result a possible double-descent example. This does not sweep model size, training epochs using test error, or sample size around an interpolation threshold. The comparison is recorded under fits_no_version; other property-prediction results do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study is about Deep InfoMax pretraining for materials property prediction. It does not sweep model size, epochs or sample size around an interpolation threshold. Its only double-descent content is an interpretation of one comparison (Fig. 11). That comparison sets a >10^5-parameter Site-Net against a small network on frozen features, at 50–1000 labels. It is two architectures with different inputs, not a capacity curve, so it bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors frame it as a surprising finding that Site-Net beats small models on frozen representations even with 50 labels. They say this 'appears to be an example of the double descent phenomenon', citing Nakkiran et al. They offer it as an interpretation, not a test. Their main conclusion is that Deep InfoMax pretraining adds value in low-label regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Deep InfoMax pretraining with Site-Net and compares transfer learning with fixed-representation downstream models; it does not reproduce a double-descent size, epoch, or sample-threshold sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream performance varies with task, label availability, and false-sampling strategy; these are not tests of the double-descent claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: A fine-tuned Site-Net (>10^5 parameters) achieves lower test MAE than a single-hidden-layer MLP on frozen Deep InfoMax features, at all label counts down to 50, for both formation energy and band gap. The authors interpret this as possibly double descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heavily overparameterized end-to-end models trained on very few labels (50) can generalise better than small models on frozen features. This is offered as an anecdotal, untested link to double descent.

record.problems: The double-descent interpretation is not supported by a capacity sweep or a measured interpolation threshold. Figure 11 reports box plots for aggregates (12 Site-Net models and 100 downstream models per condition), while the text gives no individual MAE values or explicit uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Other property-prediction comparisons in Figures 7, 8, and 12 concern the performance of Deep InfoMax pretraining or representations, not a tested double-descent curve or threshold.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; no test error near the interpolation threshold.
No supervised test-error curve over epochs. Fig. 6 shows self-supervised validation losses only.
Label counts 50–1000 are varied, but no non-monotonic test error near an interpolation threshold is examined.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No label-noise or regularization-tuning tests tied to a peak.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites 1912.02292 only to interpret one result. No curve over capacity exists, so no verdict is given. The reader's T6/discusses classification stands.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error peak near a training-set interpolation threshold.
No test-error curve over training epochs; the training curves shown are self-supervised loss curves.
Training-label availability is varied, but the study does not test whether increasing sample size raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes showing a risk curve past an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The study does not test label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
The study does not recast complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that removes the second descent.

rows.subject: supervised Site-Net models
rows.operation_detail: Train Site-Net models from Deep InfoMax parameters and compare their test MAE with downstream neural networks trained on fixed representations.
rows.baseline: neural networks trained on fixed Deep InfoMax representations
rows.value: Site-Net models have superior performance in all cases, including with 50 data points.
rows.note: The figure aggregates 12 Site-Net models and 100 downstream models per representation-learning condition. The text reports the qualitative comparison but not individual MAE values. The authors describe this as a possible double-descent example; the comparison does not establish a curve over model capacity.
rows.check: Compares two different pipelines (fine-tuned Site-Net vs. a small MLP on a frozen representation), not a model-size sweep. No test-error peak or interpolation threshold is measured. It also mixes transfer vs. representation settings, and both random and DIM initialisations appear in Fig. 11. Linking to none is correct.
